readingInstruction: Read Colossians 3:18-4:18. Paul gives instructions for households and for the church’s witness, then ends with a long list of greetings. Notice the Christ-centered grounds of each command and the picture of the church as a network of friends and coworkers.
settingTheScene: Paul has described the new life in Christ in general terms. Now he applies it to the most ordinary relationships of daily life: marriage, parents and children, work. He addresses each party in the relationship, treating all as accountable to the Lord. This is a significant feature: the instructions about households, which echo Ephesians 5 and 6, give moral responsibility to all, including children and slaves, and warn masters. The letter ends with a list of names that shows the early church as a living community.
observation: “Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them” (3:19).
“Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (3:23).
“Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” (4:1).
“Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving” (4:2).
“At the same time pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ” (4:3).
“Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (4:6).
“Remember my chains. Grace be with you” (4:18).
interpretation:
The household code in Colossians is shorter than in Ephesians but follows the same pattern. “Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.” The word for “harsh” means bitter or embittered. The husband’s role is love, not domination. “Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.” Discouragement is a real danger in children, and fathers are responsible not to cause it.

To slaves, Paul gives the longest instruction. “Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not with eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ.” This is a transformative vision of work, which we will explore on the doctrinal pause. “For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.” Then to masters: “treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.” Paul does not endorse slavery. He addresses people within a social system and weakens it from within, as Philemon will show.

Paul then calls the church to prayer and witness. “Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.” He asks for prayer for himself and his coworkers: “that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison, that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.” Imprisoned, he does not pray for release but for opportunities to preach. And the church’s own witness: “Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.” Gracious, not flat; seasoned, not bland.

The closing section is a roll call. Tychicus, “a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord,” will tell them everything about Paul, with Onesimus, “who is one of you.” Aristarchus, Mark (the cousin of Barnabas, now restored to Paul’s favor), Jesus called Justus. Epaphras, who is “always struggling on your behalf in his prayers.” Luke the beloved physician, and Demas, who will later desert him (2 Timothy 4:10). Nympha and the church in her house. And a message for Archippus: “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.” The letter ends: “I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.” Behind the doctrine are people with names and stories.
connection: Ephesians 5:22 to 6:9 is the parallel. 1 Peter 2:18 to 3:7 also addresses households. Philemon applies the teaching to a specific case. Acts 12:12 and 15:36-41 tell of Mark. Acts 20:4 mentions Tychicus. 2 Timothy 4:10-11 mentions Demas and Luke. Philemon 23-24 repeats several of these names. Revelation 3:14-22 addresses Laodicea. Proverbs 15:1 and 25:11 speak of wise speech. Luke 12:35-48 speaks of service to the master.
application:
Name the people in your life whom you serve in a relationship of authority or dependence. Treat each as someone who answers to the Lord.

Pray for a door for the gospel with someone this week. Pray also for your speech to be gracious and salty.

Write a note of thanks to a faithful fellow worker, like Tychicus.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you do whatever you do heartily, as for him.
Ask him to bless your household and your workplace.
Ask him to give you wisdom and gracious words.
